newsitem.title: USA: Crews unloading cargo on capsized Mississippi barge.
newsitem.headline: Crews unloading cargo on capsized Mississippi barge.

text.p: Workers on Monday began unloading volatile cargo of benzene and gasoline from a capsized barge wedged against a mainline levee on the flood-swollen Mississippi River, the Coast Guard said.

The process of transferring the cargo to another barge, called lightering, was expected to be completed by 11 a.m. EST (1600 GMT) Tuesday, Lt. Cheri Ben-Iesau told Reuters. After the barge is emptied, cranes will be used to right it before the river can be fully reopened to marine traffic, she said.
"They pumped in nitrogen to lessen any risk of explosion and it seems to be going smoothly," she said. "Safety is the number-one issue for the whole operation."

Federal and state officials struggled through the weekend with ways to remove the volatile petro-chemicals after a temporary injunction in state court forced them to scrap plans to drill into the overturned hull.

Officials with the Atchafalaya Basin Levee District won the temporary injunction after claiming the drilling increased the risk of explosion, which could knock out a section of the mainline levee protecting the west bank of river.
A full hearing on the injunction was to be held later Monday, but the issue was moot after unloading began.
Lightering the barge by using existing but submerged valves was delayed Sunday after a plume of the benzene mix leaked from a valve being replaced, Coast Guard spokesman Chris Haley told Reuters.
By daylight Monday, 27 tows, involving numerous barges, were backed up waiting to move downriver, Haley said. Nineteen barges moved upriver during the night.
Marine traffic in the area was restricted to one way, one vessel or tow at a time past the capsized barge. Southbound traffic was allowed only during daylight hours.
The Coast Guard reported just one minor incident of runaway barges on the river over the weekend near Convent, Louisiana, and said the barges were quickly corraled.

A mobile home spotted floating downriver toward Baton Rouge was pushed onto the bank by a tug to keep it away from vessel traffic, a spokesman said. "We have no idea where it came from, but no one was inside."
In the past week several incidents blamed on the high water's swift current closed the river in sections from Baton Rouge to the mouth of the river at Southwest Pass.
River traffic at Baton Rouge has been hampered since a string of 25 barges under tow hit a bridge on March 17. Two rock barges sank, one is missing and the third capsized.
